item.title: When Are Monomial Symmetric Polynomials Hard?
item.description: arXiv:2610.25181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a partition $\boldsymbol{\lambda} = (\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)$ and $n\ge r$, the monomial symmetric polynomial is defined as $$m_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}(x_1,\ldots,x_n) := \sum x_{i_1}^{\lambda_1} x_{i_2}^{\lambda_2} \cdots x_{i_r}^{\lambda_r},$$ where the sum ranges over all distinct monomials obtained by assigning the parts of $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ to pairwise distinct variables. We establish an almost-complete dichotomy for the complexity of the monomial symmetric polynomials $m_{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}$: If a family of partitions contains polynomially many distinct parts, then the corresponding monomial symmetric polynomials (on sufficiently many variables) are VNP-complete. If the number of distinct parts is constant, the family admits polynomial-size circuits. Thus the only remaining gap concerns the intermediate regime where the number of distinct parts grows subpolynomially. As part of our proof, we use combinatorial properties of matching polynomials to establish VNP-hardness of the perfect matching polynomial for blow-up graphs; these are graphs with non-generic edge-weights that are obtained by "blowing up" a smaller graph. We reduce these matching polynomials to monomial-symmetric polynomials by combining classical techniques from algebraic complexity theory with structural properties of Sidon sets.
item.dc:creator: Markus Bl\"aser, Radu Curticapean, Sagnik Dutta, Gorav Jindal

item.title: Faster Deterministic Integer Root Finding for Integer Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2608.00668v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a deterministic algorithm for finding all integer roots of a square-free polynomial $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ of degree $n$ with $\lVert f\rVert_\infty<2^b$. The running time is $$ \tilde{O}(n^{3/2}b), $$ improving the $\tilde{O}(n^2b)$ bound of Harvey and Hittmeir (Research in Number Theory, 2022). The algorithm follows the classical $p$-adic framework: find roots modulo a prime $p$, lift them modulo a high power of $p$, and verify the lifted candidates. The main new idea is to avoid searching for a prime for which $f\bmod p$ is square-free. Instead, we find a prime for which the total multiplicity of repeated roots modulo $p$ is small. This requires lifting repeated roots, which we handle using a weighted lifting tree. We also give a faster deterministic candidate-verification algorithm: given $n$ candidate integers smaller in absolute value than $2^b$, we decide which are roots of $f$ in $$ \tilde{O}(nb+\min(n^2,nb^2)) $$ bit operations. Together, these ingredients give the first deterministic subquadratic-in-$n$ improvement for integer root finding in the square-free case.
item.dc:creator: Itamar Nir

item.title: Compiling Expert Procedures into Verified Programs: When a Small Model Is Enough
item.description: arXiv:2610.19148v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In procedural tool-use domains, how much of the gap between base models is procedure rather than capability? We build an explicit program from a teacher's traces and run it in front of unchanged small models, including an 8B model. The construction, PLVR , takes the reasoning traces of a teacher, Kimi-K3, clusters their segments to locate recurring operations, has a frontier model author one typed primitive per operation, each run by a small frozen model and assembles the program by A* search over a mined rule library, under a reference-action objective. At inference the program takes one of two forms: for troubleshooting and tool search it produces the chain of thought the student would otherwise generate for itself, and the student acts on it; for multi-turn tool matching the student proposes each action and the program checks, repairs, or retries it before it goes out. On the official tau2-Bench Retail and Telecom test sets and on LiveMCPBench, with three Nemotron base models and the same program for each, the answer depends on the domain. On Telecom, Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2% under the program, and every Nemotron student reaches 93.3-94.4%, against at most 58.2% for fine-tuning on the same traces, prompt optimisation of the student, or two token-matched baselines. With Granite-4.2-8B as the student, the program is within 2 to 3 points of the Nemotron students on Telecom and within 3 on Retail, and 3 to 13 points below them on LiveMCPBench: where the domain is procedural an 8B student is enough, and on tool search the student still matters. On Retail and LiveMCPBench the program is competitive with the best baseline. The spread between base models shrinks from about 7 points to about 2, averaged over the suites, with no weights changed.
item.dc:creator: Vishvesh Bhat, Asad Aali, Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin
